editorial.headline: Translation Is Fully Foreign-Open Nationally—But Not for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This code gives translation and interpreting a national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling, while Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium currently stops PMA registration there.
editorial.body:
A foreign investor cannot register this translation and interpreting activity in Bali today. That is the decisive local fact, even though the activity is nationally open to foreign investment with a 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. The contrast is not cosmetic: national openness defines the position across Indonesia, while Bali’s PMA restriction determines whether this activity can be registered on the island.

The activity itself is the professional work of translating and interpreting across languages, including sign language, whether delivered orally or in writing. Its substance is not merely replacing one word with another. The recorded scope expressly reaches translation from a source language into a target language with attention to equivalent terminology, sense of language and culture. In practice, that framing places linguistic judgment at the centre of the activity: the registered business is concerned with carrying meaning accurately between languages and communicative contexts.

The code is open across the full recorded range of business scales: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. It therefore accommodates a translation or interpreting business at any of those scales under the national position. For PMA, the national ceiling is 100%, and the status is TERBUKA. There is no national foreign-share cap below full ownership in this record. A business considering registration should nevertheless distinguish that national setting from the place where it intends to operate, because the Bali position is separately and explicitly restrictive.

In Bali, the record marks the activity as BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO and confirms that it is blocked for PMA registration. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, its OSS risk classification is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope; Bali’s moratorium blocks PMA for those risk categories. The moratorium is island-wide and permanent, and the record dates the applicable block to May 2026. The result is straightforward: national rules allow foreign ownership up to 100% for this activity, but Bali does not presently permit PMA registration for it. For a founder, that is the line that matters before treating national openness as a Bali operating route.
